title: MoP-JEPA: Fixing JEPA's Blind Spot for Branching Futures
hook: A single deterministic predictor can't represent a fork in the road — it averages the branches into a state that matches nowhere. This paper proves it, then fixes it with one head per future.
key_points: JEPA world models predict the next latent state with one deterministic predictor trained by regression — which, at a stochastic branching point, collapses to the conditional mean of the possible next states: a point between them that matches no real state.
Proven mathematically for both deterministic and gated mixture-of-expert predictors — the collapse isn't a training bug, it's structural.
MoP-JEPA's hard-assigned predictors instead converge to a quantizer of the transition distribution — one head per successor mode, enumerable in a single forward pass.
On OGBench, planning over single-predictor rollouts succeeds 2-9% of the time; planning over MoP-JEPA's predicted modes reaches up to 85%.

Ships a verification protocol (codebook control, shuffled-context test, transition-precision guards) specifically to rule out the model getting credit for routes through transitions that don't actually exist.
content_html: World models built on JEPA predict the future by regressing to the next latent state. That works fine when the future is predictable — but real environments branch, and this paper proves that a single deterministic predictor mathematically cannot represent a fork: it converges to the conditional mean of the possible outcomes, a point that corresponds to no actual state.
extra_html: The authors prove this collapse holds for both plain deterministic predictors and gated mixture-of-experts predictors — it's not a training artifact, it's structural. Their fix, MoP-JEPA, hard-assigns predictor heads to distinct successor modes instead of blending them, so the model converges to a quantizer of the transition distribution: one head per branch, all enumerable in a single forward pass, which is exactly the interface a planner needs. On OGBench's offline maze data, planning over single-predictor rollouts succeeds only 2-9% of the time; planning over MoP-JEPA's predicted modes reaches up to 85%, beating deterministic, gated-MoE, and variational alternatives on every task. Because multi-prediction setups can look good by accident — crediting routes through transitions that don't actually exist — the paper also ships a verification protocol (codebook controls, shuffled-context tests, transition-precision guards) to rule that out. The takeaway: a world model's ability to plan hinges on correctly representing multimodal futures, and a hard-assigned mixture of predictors is a minimal, verifiable way to do it. Zhi Song and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a single deterministic JEPA predictor fail at a stochastic branching transition?
flashcards.back_html: Trained by latent regression, it converges to the conditional mean of the possible successor states — a point between the true branches that corresponds to no real state at all, so it can't represent the fork.

flashcards.prompt: How does MoP-JEPA's hard-assigned predictor mixture avoid this collapse?

choices.text: Each predictor head is assigned to one successor mode, converging to a quantizer of the transition distribution rather than an average
It adds more layers to the same single deterministic predictor
It removes the predictor entirely and plans over raw pixels
It trains predictors with a higher learning rate

flashcards.explanation_html: Instead of one predictor regressing to an average, MoP-JEPA hard-assigns each predictor head to a distinct successor mode — one head per branch, enumerable in a single forward pass, which a planner can consume directly.
